The basis \vartheta_p\_pin L_sV is uniquely characterised as the set of elements of whsV^S_q which are atomic with respect to the scattering atlas. For sV=sX, this is the same as the set of elements of whsX^S_q which are atomic with respect to the principal coefficient scattering atlas. For generic Q in L_sA^prin,bbR (for the sX case) or L_sA,bbR (for the sA case), each upiota_Q(vartheta_p) is positive and p-pointed, i.e. admits an expansion upiota_Q(vartheta_p)=sum_vin L_sV^oplusc_p,v,Q(t)z^p+v where each c_p,v,Q(t)inZ_geq 0[t^pm 1]subset mathbb Z_t is a positive Laurent polynomial in t (not just t^1/D) and c_p,0,Q(t)=1. Each c_p,v,Q(t) is moreover pre-Lefschetz (cf. S ), bar-invariant (i.e. c_p,v,Q(t^-1)=c_p,v,Q(t)), and satisfies c_p,v,Q(-t)=pm c_p,v,Q(t), where the sign depends only on v and p (cf. Proposition ). For p_1,p_2,pin L_sV, let upalpha(p_1,p_2;p)in mathbb Z_t denote the corresponding structure constant, i.e., vartheta_p_1vartheta_p_2=sum_pin L_sV upalpha(p_1,p_2;p) vartheta_p. Then each upalpha(p_1,p_2;p)inbbZ_t is positive (we thus call the theta basis ``strongly positive''). Furthermore, upalpha(p_1,p_2;p_1+p_2)=t^omega(p_1,p_2), and upalpha(p_1,p_2;p)=0 whenever pnotin p_1+p_2+L_sV^oplus.

The theta functions form a topological mathbb Z_t-module basis for sV_q^can, and they form an ordinary mathbb Z_t-module basis if and only if the corresponding classical theta functions form a mathbb Z-module basis for the mathbb Z-algebra sV^can which they generate.
If sV_q has enough global monomials (cf.

In particular, we then have sV_q^up subset sV_q^can.
item We have the equality sV_q^mid=sV_q^can, i.e., Theta_sV^mid=L_sV, if and only if the corresponding equality holds in the classical setting.
So if we furthermore have that sV_q has enough global monomials, then the full quantum Fock--Goncharov conjecture holds, by which we mean that sV_q^mid=sV_q^up=sV_q^can.

Corollary for the precise statement).
In addition, sV_q^can subset whsV_q^up, the formal quantum upper cluster algebra defined in S .

More generally, the adjoint action of any path-ordered product associated to fD^sV_q (or sD^sA_q^prin when sV=sX) respects the K_sV-grading on whsV_q^S.
Furthermore, the theta functions are homogeneous with respect to the K_sV-grading on whsV_q^S.
item Suppose that Uplambda satisfies the compatibility condition for all iin I (not just iin Isetminus F).
Then the map B_1 induces homomorphisms B_1colon whsX_q^Srar whsA_q^S and B_1colon sX_q^*rar sA_q^* for *=ord, mid, up, or can.
Furthermore, for any pin L_sX, we have B_1(vartheta_p)=vartheta_B_1(p).
item For uin H_sV, pin L_sV, and generic Q in L_sV,bbR, we have upiota_Q(vartheta_u+p)=uptau_u(upiota_Q(vartheta_p)).
In particular, for uin H_sV, upiota_Q(vartheta_u)=z^u for all generic Q, and so vartheta_uin sV^ord_q.

\[
f_pf_{p'}=\sum_{v\in p+p'+L^{\oplus}}a(p,p';v)f_v
\]
for certain $a(p,p';v)\in \Bbbk_t$.  Let $A$ denote the $\Bbbk_t$-algebra spanned by formal sums $\sum_{v\in w+L^{\oplus}}b_v\mathscr{F}_v$, for various $w\in L$ and some collection of symbols $\{\mathscr{F}_v\}_{v\in L}$, with structure constants given by $a(p,p';v)$, i.e. for coefficients $b_v,c_v\in \Bbbk_t$ we define
\[
\left(\sum_{v\in w+L^{\oplus}}b_v\mathscr{F}_v \right)\left( \sum_{v\in w'+L^{\oplus}}c_v\mathscr{F}_v\right)=\sum_{v\in w+w'+L^{\oplus}}\sum_{\substack{u\in w+L^{\oplus}\\u'\in w'+L^{\oplus}}}a(u,u';v)b_u c_{u'}\mathscr{F}_{v}
\]

First, assume that $p(t)$ is bar-invariant.  We can write $p(t)=\upalpha(t)+\upbeta(t)$ where $\upalpha(t)$ is odd and $\upbeta(t)$ is even, and both are bar-invariant.  Since 
\begin{align*}
\log\left[\mathbb{E}(-\upalpha(t)-\upbeta(t))\right]=&\log\left[\mathbb{E}(-\upalpha(t))\mathbb{E}(-\upbeta(t))\right]\\
=&\log\left[\mathbb{E}(-\upalpha(t))\right]+\log\left[\mathbb{E}(-\upbeta(t))\right],
\end{align*}
it suffices to prove the claim for both $\upalpha(t)$ and $\upbeta(t)$ separately.  Write $\upalpha(t)=\sum_i \upalpha_it^i$.  Then by \eqref{EEoddPsi} we have
\begin{align*}
    \log[\mathbb{E}(\upalpha(t))]=&\log\left(\prod_{r=0}^{\infty}\prod_{i\in\mathbb{Z}\lvert   \upalpha_i\neq 0}\Psi_{t^{2^r}}(t^{2^ri}z^{2^rv})^{\upalpha_i}\right)\\
    =&-\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}\lvert \upalpha_i\neq 0}\upalpha_i\mathrm{Li}(-t^{2^ri}z^{2^rv};t^{2^r})
\end{align*}
and the statement follows from
\[
\mathrm{Li}(-t^{2^ri}z^{2^rv};t^{2^r})_{t\mapsto t^{-1}}=\mathrm{Li}(-t^{-2^ri}z^{2^rv};t^{2^r})
\]
and $\upalpha_i=\upalpha_{-i}$.  The proof for $\upbeta(t)$ is similar, but simpler.

The reverse implication follows from the fact that the $z^v$ coefficient of $\log(\mathbb{E}(-p(t)z^v))$ is precisely $p(t)/(1)_t$.

nodes.statement: For the statements regarding p_i(t) being positive or pL, we will in S inductively reduce to the case of just two initial walls. Then Corollary and Proposition will prove the positivity and pL statements, respectively, for these two-wall cases. For bar-invariance, recall from Lemma that p(t) is bar-invariant if and only if log(E(-p(t)z^v)) is bar-invariant. Note that we can view fg=fg_L_0^+,omega as a Lie algebra over Bbbk rather than Bbbk[t^pm 1], and then we can consider the Lie subalgebra fg^bar (over Bbbk) consisting of the bar-invariant elements. So the bar-invariance of the Laurent polynomials p_i(t) implies that we can view fD_in as a scattering diagram over fg^bar, and then applying Theorem over fg^bar yields fD defined over fg^bar as well. Then each p_fd(t) must be bar-invariant, as desired.

For the statements regarding $p_i(t)$ being positive or pL, we will in \S \ref{PosSect} inductively reduce to the case of just two initial walls.  Then Corollary \ref{2WallPos} and Proposition \ref{2WallpL} will prove the positivity and pL statements, respectively, for these two-wall cases.

For bar-invariance, recall from Lemma \ref{log_barinv} that $p(t)$ is bar-invariant if and only if $\log(\mathbb{E}(-p(t)z^v))$ is bar-invariant.
Note that we can view $\f{g}=\f{g}_{L_0^+,\omega}$ as a Lie algebra over $\Bbbk$ rather than $\Bbbk[t^{\pm 1}]$, and then we can consider the Lie subalgebra $\f{g}^{\mathrm{bar}}$ (over $\Bbbk$) consisting of the bar-invariant elements.  So the bar-invariance of the Laurent polynomials $p_i(t)$ implies that we can view $\f{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ as a scattering diagram over $\f{g}^{\mathrm{bar}}$, and then applying Theorem \ref{KSGS}  over $\f{g}^{\mathrm{bar}}$ yields $\f{D}$ defined over $\f{g}^{\mathrm{bar}}$ as well.  Then each $p_{\f{d}}(t)$ must be bar-invariant, as desired.

Given $n\in L^{+}\subset L$, let $\updelta(n)\in \bb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ denote the largest number $k$ such that $n\in kL^+$ as defined in \eqref{kNplus}.  We extend this to $\updelta\colon L^{\oplus}\rar \bb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ by taking $\updelta(0)\coloneqq 0$.  Note that $\updelta(n_1+n_2)\geq \updelta(n_1)+\updelta(n_2)$ for any $n_1,n_2\in L^{\oplus}$. 


Since $\f{g}$ is $L_0^+$-graded and acts on $\Bbbk_t\llb L\rrb$ by $L$-graded $\Bbbk_t$-derivations, we see that for any $v\in L_0^+$, $f\in \hat{G}_v^{\parallel}$, $c\in \Bbbk[t^{\pm 1}]$, and $p\in L$, the element $\mathrm{Ad}_f(cz^p)\in \Bbbk_t\llb L\rrb$ must have the form
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Ad}_f(cz^p)=cz^p\left(1+\sum_{k\in \bb{Z}_{>0}}c_k z^{kv}\right)
\end{align*}
for some collection of coefficients $c_k\in \Bbbk[t^{\pm 1}]$.  From this it is clear that if $\upgamma$ is a broken line with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$, then $v_{\upgamma}\in p+L^{\oplus}$.  Furthermore, we see that $v_{\upgamma}=p$ if and only if $\upgamma$ is the unique straight broken line with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$, and in this case we have $c_{\upgamma}z^{\upgamma}=z^p$.  In particular, once we show that $\vartheta_{p,\mathcal{Q}}$ is well-defined, it will immediately follow that it has the form given in \eqref{pointed}.

Now to show that $\uptheta_{p,\mathcal{Q}}$ is well-defined, we need to show that for each fixed $v\in p+L^+$, there are only finitely many broken lines $\upgamma$ with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$ and with $v_{\upgamma}=v$.  
Suppose $(\f{d},f_{\f{d}})\in \f{D}\setminus \f{D}_{\updelta(v-p)}$.  Then if $(\f{d},f_{\f{d}})$ contributes to a bend of a broken line $\upgamma$ with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$, we have $\updelta(v_{\upgamma}-p)>\updelta(v-p)$.  Thus, it suffices to restrict to the finite scattering diagram $\f{D}_{\updelta(v-p)}$.

By starting at $\uptau=0$ and flowing backwards, we see that a broken line $\upgamma$ with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$ and $v_{\upgamma}=v$ is uniquely determined by its kinks, i.e., by the data of where it bends and the degrees $\updelta$ which it bends by.  But since each kink increases $\updelta(v_{\upgamma}-p)$, such $\upgamma$ can have at most $\updelta(v-p)$ many kinks, and since $\f{D}_{\updelta(v-p)}$ is finite, there are only finitely many places where $\upgamma$ can cross a wall of $\f{D}_{\updelta(v-p)}$.  This shows that there are only finitely many such $\upgamma$, as desired, and so $\vartheta_{p,\mathcal{Q}}$ is well-defined.


Finally, since \eqref{pointed} says that $\vartheta_{p,\mathcal{Q}}$ is $p$-pointed, Lemma \ref{PointedBasis} tells us that $\Theta_{\mathcal{Q}}$ is indeed a topological basis for $\Bbbk_t\llb L\rrb$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{bar_prop}
Let $v\in L_0^+$, $p\in L$, and $\epsilon\coloneqq \mathrm{sgn}\omega(v,p)$.  Suppose $p(t)$ is a bar-invariant positive Laurent polynomial in $t$.  Then $\mathrm{Ad}_{\mathbb{E}\left(-\epsilon p(t)z^v\right)}(z^p)$ is bar-invariant.

We give V a cohomological grading by placing the ith weight space with respect to the action of h in cohomological degree i. Then V acquires a Koplus Z grading, and upchi_K,t(V)=sum_nin K f_n(t)x^n with each f_n(t) a Lefschetz type polynomial. Let V_i be the irreducible i-dimensional sl_2-representation (without any K-grading). Then the characteristic function upchi_t(V) of V_i is [i]_t, and so the characteristic function of a KoplusZ-graded vector space V satisfies the condition that all f_n(t) defined as in are of Lefschetz type if and only if V can be constructed from a K-graded sl_2-representation in this way. Now we deal with two cases. If a is odd, the z^nv coefficient of Exp_-t,z([a]_t[|b|]_tt^bz^v) is equal to t^nbupchi_t(bigwedge^n(V_aotimes V_|b|)) by (), and so the z^p+nv coefficient of () is upchi_t(bigwedge^n(V_aotimes V_|b|)). In particular, this coefficient is of Lefschetz type since it arises from an integrable sl_2-representation. Similarly, if a is even, then by () again, the z^p+nv coefficient of () is equal to upchi_t(Sym^n(V_aotimes V_|b|)), and again of Lefschetz type.

nodes.raw_latex:
Define $P$ to be the span over $\mathbb{R}$ of $v_1,\ldots,v_s$.  We define $\overline{\lambda}$ on $P$ by 
\[
\overline{\lambda}\left(\sum_{i=1}^s a_iv_i,\sum_{i=1}^s b_iv_i\right)=\lambda(a,b).
\]
This gives a well-defined bilinear form by linear independence of $v_1,\ldots, v_s$, and we moreover have
\[
\omega(v,v')=\overline{\lambda}(v,v')-\overline{\lambda}(v',v)
\]
for $v,v'\in P$.


Let $\upgamma$ be a broken line with ends $(p,\mathcal{Q})$, and let $c_j(t)z^{p+w_i}$ be the monomials associated to the straight line segments of $\upgamma$.  We assume for all $j\leq k$ that the parity of $c_j(t)$ is given by $\omega(p,w_j)+\overline{\lambda}(w_j,w_j)$.  Assume that $\upgamma(\uptau_k)$ lies on the wall
\begin{align}
(\f{d},\mathbb{E}(-d(t)z^{v_{\f{d}}})).
\end{align}
Then by Theorem \ref{parity_cor}, $\mathrm{par}(d(t))=\overline{\lambda}(v_{\f{d}},v_{\f{d}})+1$.

Combining Lemma \ref{parity_prop} and the inductive hypothesis, writing
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Ad}_{\mathbb{E}(-\epsilon d(t)z^{v_{\f{d}}})}(c_k(t)z^{p+w_k})=\sum_{i\geq 0}g_i(t)z^{p+w_k+iv_{\f{d}}}
\end{align*}
we calculate that (mod $2$) 
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{par}(g_i(t))\equiv&\mathrm{par}(c_k(t))+i(\omega(v_{\f{d}},p+w_k)+\mathrm{par}(d(t))+1)\\\equiv&[\omega(p,w_k)+\overline{\lambda}(w_k,w_k)]+[i\omega(v_{\f{d}},p+w_k)+i\overline{\lambda}(v_{\f{d}},v_{\f{d}})]\\
\equiv&[\omega(p,w_k)+\omega(iv_{\f{d}},p+w_k)] + [\overline{\lambda}(w_k+iv_{\f{d}},w_k+iv_{\f{d}}) - \omega(w_k,iv_{\f{d}})]\\
\equiv&\omega(p,w_k+i v_{\f{d}})+\overline{\lambda}(w_k+iv_{\f{d}},w_k+iv_{\f{d}})
\end{align*}
as required.

nodes.statement: Theorem tells us that the quantum theta functions are universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas. To show atomicity, it thus suffices to show that for any fin A universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas, the expansion f=sum_pin L a_p vartheta_p has positive integer coefficients. For any pin L, one can choose a positive integer k which is large enough to ensure that that pnotin p'+kL_0^+ for any p' with a_p'neq 0. Then for Q sharing a chamber of fD_k with p, the only possible broken line with respect to fD, with ends (p',Q) for a_p'neq 0, and with v_upgamma=p is the straight broken line with attached monomial z^p. It follows that for Q sufficiently close to p, a_p is equal to c_p in the formal Laurent series expansion upiota_Q(f)=sum_pin L c_p z^p. This is indeed positive by the universal positivity assumption on f.
nodes.raw_latex:
Theorem \ref{qPosLoc} tells us that the quantum theta functions are universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas.  To show atomicity, it thus suffices to show that for any $f\in A$ universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas, the expansion $f=\sum_{p\in L} a_p \vartheta_p$ has positive integer coefficients.  For any $p\in L$, one can choose a positive integer $k$ which is large enough to ensure that that $p\notin p'+kL_0^+$ for any $p'$ with $a_{p'}\neq 0$.  Then for $\mathcal{Q}$ sharing a chamber of $\f{D}_k$ with $p$, the only possible broken line with respect to $\f{D}$, with ends $(p',\mathcal{Q})$ for $a_{p'}\neq 0$, and with $v_{\upgamma}=p$ is the straight broken line with attached monomial $z^p$.   
It follows that for $\mathcal{Q}$ sufficiently close to $p$, $a_p$ is equal to $c_p$ in the formal Laurent series expansion $\upiota_{\mathcal{Q}}(f)=\sum_{p\in L} c_p z^p$.  This is indeed positive by the universal positivity assumption on $f$.

To show atomicity, it thus suffices to show that for any fin A universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas, the expansion f=sum_pin L a_p vartheta_p has positive integer coefficients. For any pin L, one can choose a positive integer k which is large enough to ensure that that pnotin p'+kL_0^+ for any p' with a_p'neq 0. Then for Q sharing a chamber of fD_k with p, the only possible broken line with respect to fD, with ends (p',Q) for a_p'neq 0, and with v_upgamma=p is the straight broken line with attached monomial z^p. It follows that for Q sufficiently close to p, a_p is equal to c_p in the formal Laurent series expansion upiota_Q(f)=sum_pin L c_p z^p. This is indeed positive by the universal positivity assumption on f.

The equality is now equivalent to the condition that Uplambda^prin|_B_1,prin((N,0)) is given as in . It is clear that upxi is injective and thus extends to the skew-fields of fractions. Since the mutations are automorphisms of the corresponding formal quantum cluster algebras, it suffices to check that upxi and rho commute with the mutations associated to the initial seed (because the same formulas define upxi and rho in the coordinate system associated to any other seed). First we must check that $\upxi$ and $\rho$ induce well-defined maps of the quantum torus algebras.  For $\upxi$, this means checking that 
\begin{align}\label{LambdaPrinB}
    \Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}(\upxi(n_1),\upxi(n_2))=B(n_1,n_2).
\end{align}
By the definition of $\upxi$, the left-hand side of \eqref{LambdaPrinB} is $\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}((B_1(n_1),n_1),(B_1(n_2),n_2))$, which by \eqref{pi1prin} equals $\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}(B^{\mathrm{prin}}_1(n_1,0),B^{\mathrm{prin}}_1(n_2,0))$.  The equality \eqref{LambdaPrinB} is now equivalent to the condition that $\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}|_{B_{1,\mathrm{prin}}((N,0))}$ is given as in \eqref{LambdaPrin}.  It is clear that $\upxi$ is injective and thus extends to the skew-fields of fractions.  Since $\upxi(e_i)=B_1^{\mathrm{prin}}(e_i)$, we see that $\upxi(\upsigma_{S,\s{X}})= \upsigma_{S^{\mathrm{prin}},\s{A}}$, and so $\upxi$ extends to the completions as well.

Similarly, the condition for $\rho$ to induce a well-defined map of quantum torus algebras is just that $\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}((m_1,n_1),(m_2,n_2))=\Uplambda(\rho(m_1,n_1),\rho(m_2,n_2))$, and this is the condition we imposed. \label{nonskew}
Throughout this article, we assume that all seeds are skew-symmetric, i.e., that the bilinear form $B$ is skew-symmetric.  More generally though, $B$ might be merely ``skew-symmetrizable,'' i.e., of the form $B(e_i,e_j)=d_j\upbeta(e_i,e_j)$ for some skew-symmetric $\bb{Q}$-valued form $\upbeta$ and some numbers $d_j\in \bb{Q}_{> 0}$ such that $B(e_i,e_j)\in \bb{Z}$ whenever $i$ and $j$ are not both in $F$.  Then following \cite{BZ} for the $\s{A}$-side and \cite{FG1} for the $\s{X}$-side, the constructions of the quantum cluster algebras change in the following ways.  The maps $B_1$ and $B_2$ are defined in the same way using $B$, but the quantum torus algebra $\s{X}_q^S$ is defined using $\upbeta$, i.e., $\s{X}_q^S\coloneqq \Bbbk_t^{\upbeta}[N]$. The compatibility condition \eqref{Lambda} is changed to $\Uplambda(\cdot,B_1(e_i))=\frac{1}{d_i}e_i$.  The mutations $\upmu_j^{\s{A}}$ and $\upmu_j^{\s{X}}$ are defined using 
$\mathrm{Ad}_{\Psi_{t^{1/d_i}}(z^{B_1(e_i)})^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{Ad}_{\Psi_{t^{1/d_i}}(z^{e_i})^{-1}}$, respectively.  Then as suggested in \cite[\S 4.2]{Man3}, the appropriate initial scattering diagrams seem to be $ \f{D}^{\s{A}_q}_{\mathrm{in}}\coloneqq \{(e_i^{\perp},\Psi_{t^{1/d_i}}(z^{e_i}))\colon i\in I\setminus F\}$ and
$\f{D}^{\s{X}_q}_{\mathrm{in}}\coloneqq \{(B_2(e_i)^{\perp},\Psi_{t^{1/d_i}}(z^{B_1(e_i)}))\colon i\in I\setminus F, B_2(e_i)\neq 0\}$, because crossing these walls recovers the quantum mutations associated to the initial seed as defined in \cite{BZ} and \cite{FG1}, respectively (defining these scattering diagrams in a way compatible with $\lim_{t\rar 1}$ requires some careful modifications to the definition of $\f{g}$).  However, it is suspected that positivity for quantum theta functions will fail in this general setup --- in rank $2$, the quantum theta functions are expected to agree with the quantum greedy bases, and positivity for some greedy basis elements (outside the cluster complex) is known to fail, cf. \cite[end of \S 3]{LLRZpnas}.

It is straightforward to check that applying $\lim_{t\rar 1}$ to $\f{D}^{\s{A}_q}$ yields the corresponding classical scattering diagram $\f{D}_{\mathrm{in},\textbf{s}}$ of \cite{GHKK}.  The claim thus follows for $\wh{\s{A}}_q^{\mathrm{prin},S}$, since for these cases the \cite{GHKK} theta functions are constructed directly from the broken lines corresponding to $\lim_{t\rar 1} \f{D}_q^{\s{A}_t^{\mathrm{prin}}}=\f{D}_{\mathrm{in},\textbf{s}^{\mathrm{prin}}}$.  For $\wh{\s{A}}_q^{S}$, \cite[\S 7.2]{GHKK} constructs the theta functions by applying the classical analog of our map $\rho$ from Lemma \ref{xirho}.\footnote{The reason that \cite{GHKK} does not just directly construct the theta functions for the $\s{A}$-space using $\f{D}_{\mathrm{in},\textbf{s}}$ is that they allow $\s{A}$-spaces for which their ``injectivity assumption'' is not satisfied, i.e., for which there is no compatible pair $\Uplambda$, hence no quantization.  In such cases, there might not exist a strictly convex cone $\upsigma_{S,\s{A}}$ containing the negative directions of the initial walls.}  Lemma \ref{prin2A} states that $\rho$ takes quantum theta functions to quantum theta functions, so the classical limits of the quantum theta functions in $\wh{\s{A}}_q$ are indeed the classical theta functions of \cite{GHKK}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition \ref{Chambers}
nodes.statement: The existence of the fan sC satisfying Properties (1) and (2) follows from the classical case because positivity implies that the set of walls is unchanged when we take the tmapsto 1 limit. Consider a wall (fd,f) of sC with associated vector v = pm psi_vecjmath^-1(B_1(e_S_vecjmath,j)) as in the statement of (3). The classical analog of (3) says that lim_trar 1 f = lim_trar 1 Psi_t(z^v). Theorem tells us that f=bbE(-p(t)z^v) for p(t) a bar-invariant Laurent polynomial in t with positive integer coefficients. By , p(1) must equal 1, and so (using positivity and bar-invariance) the only possibility is that p(t)=1, as desired. For (4), let vecjmath=(j_1,ldots,j_s), and suppose inductively that psi_vecjmath_scirc upiota_vecjmath_s=upmu^sA_vecjmath_s. By (3), we know that the wall-crossing automorphism for crossing from sC_vecjmath_s to sC_vecjmath is given by Ad^epsilon_ Psi_t(z^psi_vecjmath^-1(-epsilon v)), where v=B_1(e_S_vecjmath_s,j_s), so upmu^sA_S_vecjmath_s,j_s=Ad^-1_Psi_t(z^v). nodes.statement: The statement that each vartheta_p,Q_vecjmath is a Laurent polynomial follows from its classical analog and the positivity of broken lines --- since the classical limit has contributions from only finitely many broken lines, and applying lim_trar 1 does not cause any broken lines to vanish, the quantum theta function must consist of contributions from only finitely many broken lines as well. The claim that psi_vecjmath(vartheta_p,Q_vecjmath) = upmu^sA_S,vecjmath(vartheta_p,Q)in sA_q^S_vecjmath then follows from Theorem and Proposition (4). For the statements on cluster monomials, together show that in the classical limit, the only broken line contributing to vartheta_p,Q is the straight line with attached monomial z^p. By positivity, this is also the only broken line for the quantum analog (any others would have non-trivial classical limit), and since it has no kinks, the attached monomial must again be the initial monomial z^p.

\label{EGMdef}
One says that $\s{A}_q$ (resp., $\s{X}_q$) has \textbf{enough global monomials (EGM)} if for every $u\in N_S$ (resp., every $u\in M_S$), there exists a global monomial $g\in \s{A}_q^{\mathrm{ord}}\subset \s{A}_q^S= \Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]$ (resp. $g\in \s{X}_q^{\mathrm{ord}}\subset \s{X}_q^S=\Bbbk_t^{B}[N]$) such that $g^{\mathrm{trop}}(u)< 0$.

We now put our results together to complete the proof of Theorem \ref{MainThm}.  First, note that all broken lines, mutations, and actions of path-ordered products could be defined over $\bb{Z}_t$ rather than $\Bbbk_t$, so we may work  over $\bb{Z}_t$ as in \S \ref{MainResultsSection}.  The statement that the theta functions form a topological basis for $\wh{\s{V}}_q^S$ is part of Proposition \ref{TopBasis}.  The statement that the global monomials are elements of the theta basis is Corollary \ref{UpTheta} in the $\s{A}$ case and the proof of Proposition \ref{midX} in the $\s{X}$ case.

The fact that $\upiota_{\mathcal{Q}}(\vartheta_p)$ has coefficients in ${\mathbb Z}[t^{\pm 1}]$ instead of ${\mathbb Z}[t^{\pm 1/D}]$ was already implicit in our definition of the theta functions in \S \ref{theta-def} --- the fundamental point here is the assumption that $\omega(L_0,L)$ is contained in $\bb{Z}$ instead of just $\bb{Q}$.  That $\vartheta_p$ is $p$-pointed is given by \eqref{pointed}.  Next we note that the functions on the walls of $\f{D}^{\s{V}_q}$ are bar-invariant and pre-Lefschetz by the corresponding statements in Theorem \ref{PosScat}.  That $\vartheta_p$ is bar-invariant and pre-Lefschetz then follows as a special case of Proposition \ref{bar-pL}.  The claim regarding the parity of the coefficients is a special case of Proposition \ref{ParitProp}.

Next, positivity of the coefficients $\upalpha(p_1,p_2;p)$ is given by Theorem \ref{qPosStrong}.  Finally, atomicity is a special case of Theorem \ref{qAtomic}, with the extension to the principal coefficients scattering atlas following as in \S \ref{AtlasX}.

nodes.statement: The proof of this theorem is within the framework of cohomological Donaldson--Thomas theory. \]

First we claim that for any quasiprojective variety $X$ the degree zero intersection cohomology $\mathrm{IC}^0(X,\bb{Q})$ has a natural basis indexed by the irreducible components of $X$, which we label $X_p$ for $p$ in an indexing set $P_X$.  This follows from definitions and foundational results in intersection homology, see \cite[Chapter 4]{KiWo}.  

In a little more detail:  Firstly, the morphism from the normalization $\wt{X}\rightarrow X$ is small, so $\mathrm{IC}(X,\bb{Q})\cong \mathrm{IC}(\wt{X},\bb{Q})\cong \oplus_{p\in P_{\tilde{X}}} \mathrm{IC}(\wt{X_p},\bb{Q})$, and so it is sufficient to prove the claim under the assumption that $X$ is irreducible.  By results of Whitney \cite{Whitney}, \L ojasiewicz \cite{Loj} and Goresky \cite{Gor}, there is a Whitney stratification of $X$ by complex subvarieties, along with a triangulation of $X$ respecting the stratification.  The sum of the top degree simplices of this triangulation gives a spanning top degree class in intersection homology, i.e. a degree zero class in intersection cohomology, by Poincar\'e duality.  This proves the claim.  

Then the first equality follows from the fact that $\mathcal{M}_v^{\upzeta-st}(Q)$ is a dense open subvariety of $\mathcal{M}_v^{\upzeta-sst}(Q)$, and is irreducible, as it is a free quotient of an irreducible variety.  The second equality follows from the fact that the degree of $\mathrm{IC}\left(\mathcal{M}_v^{\upzeta-sst}(Q),\mathbb{Q}\right)$ is bounded above by $-2(\upchi_Q(v,v)-1)$, since by \eqref{dim_count} this is the real dimension of $\mathcal{M}_v^{\upzeta-sst}(Q)$.

If $Q$ is symmetric, in the sense that between any two distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ there are as many arrows from $i$ to $j$ as from $j$ to $i$, then the degenerate stability condition $\upzeta=(0,\ldots,0)$ is generic, and there is an equality
\[
\mathcal{A}_{\uptheta=0}^{\upzeta}(Q)=\mathrm{H}(\mathfrak{M}(Q),\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{vir}}.
\]
Under these conditions, Efimov \cite{Efi} proved that $\mathcal{A}_{\uptheta=0}^{\upzeta}(Q)\cong \mathbb{S}ym\left(V_{\mathrm{prim}}\otimes \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{pt}/\mathbb{C}^*,\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{vir}}\right)$ for some $V_{\mathrm{prim}}\in \mathrm{Vect}^+_K$ such that each $V_{\mathrm{prim},v}$ has finite-dimensional total cohomology.  Theorem \ref{coh_int_thm} gives a precise definition of $V_{\mathrm{prim}}$ in this case.

Theorem B in \cite{DavMei} gives the following Hodge theoretic upgrade of (\ref{CWCE}):
\[
\bigoplus_{v\in K}\mathrm{H}(\mathfrak{M}_v(Q),\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{vir}}\cong \bigotimes^{\mathrm{tw}}_{\infty \xrightarrow{\uptheta}-\infty}\mathcal{A}^{\upzeta}_{\uptheta,\mathrm{Hdg}}(Q).

\[
\mathcal{A}_{\uptheta,\mathrm{Hdg}}^{\upzeta}(Q)\subset \bigoplus_{v\in S_{\uptheta}^{\upzeta}}\mathrm{H}(\mathfrak{M}_v(Q),\mathbb{Q})\otimes \mathbb{L}^{\upchi_Q(v,v)/2}.
\]
Now the result follows from the fact that 
\[
\mathrm{H}(\mathfrak{M}_v(Q),\mathbb{Q})\cong \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{pt}/\mathrm{GL}_v,\mathbb{Q})
\]
is pure, of Tate type, and concentrated in even degrees.

Then consider any N-dimensional bbCQ-module rho, with dimension vector v satisfying \[ v_i= 1 &if iin P \\ 0 &otherwise \] and for which the action of each a_1,ldots,a_n is an isomorphism. Clearly this module is simple, and so in particular it is King-stable for any stability condition in underlinedim(rho)^perp. Let upzetain underlinedim(rho)^perp be a general stability condition. Then rho is upzeta-stable, and so M^upzeta -Kss_v(Q) is nonempty. The top degree compactly supported cohomology of this stack has, as a basis, the set of top-dimensional irreducible components; since the stack is irreducible, this cohomology is one-dimensional, and in particular nontrivial. It follows that \[ bigoplus_vin KH_c (M^upzeta -Kss_v(Q),Q)_virneq 0 \] and so by Proposition \[ int 1_ss(upzeta)neq 0. \] It follows that underlinedim(rho)^perp is covered by walls of fD_Stab, and in particular contains an incoming wall. So if there exists a cycle as above with N>1, then Q is not genteel. On the other hand, assume that Q contains no cycles that are not entirely composed of loops. Equivalently, we can label the vertices Q_0 with numbers \1,ldots,r\ in such a way that for i>j there are no arrows from i to j. Given a bbCQ-module rho, let Q_0^rho denote the vertices of Q which lie in the support of rho, and let Q^rho be the subquiver of Q consisting of these vertices and all arrows between them. Given any connected component Q' of Q^rho, let upalphain \1,ldots,r\ be the minimal number for which rho has non-trivial support rho_upalpha at the vertex upalpha. We extend rho_upalpha by zero to obtain a submodule rho'subset rho. Then B(underlinedim(rho),underlinedim(rho'))geq 0, with equality if and only if upalpha is the only vertex of Q'. Thus, rho cannot be self-semistable unless every component of Q^rho has only a single vertex (possibly with loops). So if rho is self-semistable, it must be a direct sum of representations which are supported on disjoint vertices. Suppose rho is semistable for some other stability condition upzeta. Then each summand rho_upalpha of rho must be upzeta-semistable, thus forcing upzeta to be in underlinedim(rho_upalpha)^perp for each rho_upalpha. So the locus of such upzeta lives in codimension at least two (and thus does not form a wall) unless rho is supported at a single vertex, as desired.

Let $a_n\cdots a_1$ be a cycle in $Q$, and let $P\subset Q_0$ be the set of vertices occurring as $s(a_l)$ or $t(a_l)$ for $1\leq l\leq n$.  Set $N=\lvert P\lvert$.   Then consider any $N$-dimensional $\bb{C}Q$-module $\rho$, with dimension vector $v$ satisfying
\[
v_i=\begin{cases} 1 &\textrm{if }i\in P \\
0 &\textrm{otherwise}\end{cases}
\]
and for which the action of each $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ is an isomorphism.  Clearly this module is simple, and so in particular it is King-stable for any stability condition in $\underline{\dim}(\rho)^{\perp}$.  

Let $\upzeta\in \underline{\dim}(\rho)^\perp$ be a general stability condition.  Then $\rho$ is $\upzeta$-stable, and so $\mathfrak{M}^{\upzeta -Kss}_{v}(Q)$ is nonempty.  The top degree compactly supported cohomology of this stack has, as a basis, the set of top-dimensional irreducible components; since the stack is irreducible, this cohomology is one-dimensional, and in particular nontrivial.  It follows that
\[
\bigoplus_{v\in K}\mathrm{H}_c (\mathfrak{M}^{\upzeta -Kss}_{v}(Q),\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{vir}}\neq 0
\]
and so by Proposition \ref{Apurity}
\[
\int 1_{\mathrm{ss}}(\upzeta)\neq 0.
\]
It follows that $\underline{\dim}(\rho)^{\perp}$ is covered by walls of $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$, and in particular contains an incoming wall.  So if there exists a cycle as above with $N>1$, then $Q$ is not genteel.

On the other hand, assume that $Q$ contains no cycles that are not entirely composed of loops.  Equivalently, we can label the vertices $Q_0$ with numbers $\{1,\ldots,r\}$ in such a way that for $i>j$ there are no arrows from $i$ to $j$.

Given a $\bb{C}Q$-module $\rho$, let $Q_0^{\rho}$ denote the vertices of $Q$ which lie in the support of $\rho$, and let $Q^{\rho}$ be the subquiver of $Q$ consisting of these vertices and all arrows between them.  Given any connected component $Q'$ of $Q^{\rho}$, let $\upalpha\in \{1,\ldots,r\}$ be the minimal number for which $\rho$ has non-trivial support $\rho_{\upalpha}$ at the vertex $\upalpha$.  We extend $\rho_{\upalpha}$ by zero to obtain a submodule $\rho'\subset \rho$.  Then $B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\underline{\dim}(\rho'))\geq 0$, with equality if and only if $\upalpha$ is the only vertex of $Q'$.  Thus, $\rho$ cannot be self-semistable unless every component of $Q^{\rho}$ has only a single vertex (possibly with loops).

So if $\rho$ is self-semistable, it must be a direct sum of representations which are supported on disjoint vertices.  Suppose $\rho$ is semistable for some other stability condition $\upzeta$.  Then each summand $\rho_{\upalpha}$ of $\rho$ must be $\upzeta$-semistable, thus forcing $\upzeta$ to be in $\underline{\dim}(\rho_{\upalpha})^{\perp}$ for each $\rho_{\upalpha}$.  So the locus of such $\upzeta$ lives in codimension at least two (and thus does not form a wall) unless $\rho$ is supported at a single vertex, as desired.

It will be convenient to assume that the vectors $v_i$ span $L_{\bb{R}}$.  We can always assume this after possibly extending $L_0$ to some finite-index sublattice $L'_0$ of $L$, enlarging $\upsigma$ to have full rank in $L_{\bb{R}}$, and then enlarging $V$ with a minimal set of additional vectors $v_i$ so that the resulting set $V'$ spans $L_{\bb{R}}$.   The polynomials $p_i(t)$ associated to $v_i\in V'\setminus V$ are taken to be, say, $1$.  After proving the results for this setup, one can then take the quotient by $\bigoplus_{v\in (L'_0)^+\setminus L_0^+} \f{g}_v$ to obtain the results in general.  So we now assume $V$ spans $L_{\bb{R}}$.

Recall the quiver $Q=Q(V,P)$ defined above.  
Let $K=\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{Q_0}$ be the monoid of dimension vectors for $\BQ{V,P}$.  There is a homomorphism of algebras
\[
F\colon \Bbbk_t[K]\rightarrow \Bbbk_t[L_0^{\oplus}]
\]
defined as follows.  Write $p_i(t)=\sum_l p_{i,l}t^l$.  For $(i,\upalpha)\in Q_0$ define 
\[
\upeta'_i(\upalpha)=\max\left\{ r~\colon~ \sum_{r'< r}p_{i,r'} < \upalpha,~ \mathrm{par}(r)= \mathrm{par}(p_i(t))\right\}.  
\]
For example if $p_i(t)=3t^{-2}+4+3t^2$, 
\[
(\upeta'_i(1),\ldots ,\upeta'_i(10))=(-2,-2,-2,0,0,0,0,2,2,2).
\]
We define 
\[
\upeta_i(\upalpha)=\begin{cases} \upeta'_i(\upalpha) & \textrm{if }i\leq s'\\
\upeta'_i(\upalpha)+1 &\textrm{if }s'<i\leq s.
\end{cases}
\]
Note that for all $(i,\upalpha)\in Q_0$ there is an equality 
\begin{equation}\label{eta_parity}
    \upeta_i(\upalpha)\equiv 0 \quad\textrm{ (mod $2$).} 
\end{equation}
We set 
\begin{equation*}
F(x_{i,\upalpha})=t^{\upeta_i(\upalpha)}z^{v_i}.
\end{equation*}

Passing to completions, $F$ induces a morphism $G^{\mathrm{qtr}}_Q\rightarrow G^{\mathrm{qtr}}$ which we denote by $\hat{F}$.  From \eqref{bosvfer} and \eqref{eta_parity} it follows that
\[
\hat{F}(\mathbb{E}(p(t)x^v)=\mathbb{E}(p(t)F(x^v))
\]
for all $0\neq v\in K$ and all $p(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm 1}]$.




We define a $L_0^{+}$-grading on $\f{g}_Q$ by pulling back the $L_0^{+}$-grading on the image of $F$.  Then the scattering diagram $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ for the category of $\mathbb{C}Q$-modules satisfies
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i\leq s'$ and $\upalpha\leq p_i(1)$ there is an incoming wall $(\g{i,\upalpha}^{\perp},\mathbb{E}(-x_{i,\upalpha}))$ \item
    For each $s'<i\leq s$ and $\upalpha\leq p_i(1)$ there is an incoming wall $(\g{i,\upalpha}^{\perp},\mathbb{E}(-t^{-1}x_{i,\upalpha}))$
    \item
    All walls in $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ are of the form $(\f{d},\mathbb{E}(-p_v(t)x^v))$ with $p_v(t)\in\bb{Z}_{\geq 0}[t^{\pm 1}]$ and $\f{d}\subset v^{\perp}$ for $v\in K$. 
    \item
    $\mathrm{par}(p_v(t))\equiv \upchi_Q(v,v)+1$ (mod $2$).
\end{enumerate}
The first two parts of the claim follow from Example \ref{InEx}.  The last two parts are a special case of Proposition \ref{Pos1}.  The morphism
\begin{align*}
    R\colon \mathbb{R}^{Q_0}\rightarrow &L_{0,\mathbb{R}}\\
    \g{i,\upalpha}\mapsto &v_i
\end{align*}
induces a surjection of vector spaces, with $R^*\omega=B_Q$.  As in Lemma \ref{QuotientScat}, $R$ and $F$ induce a consistent scattering diagram $(R,F)_*\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ in $L_{\bb{R}}$ over $\f{g}$, giving the desired scattering diagram.  For the statement regarding the parity of $\f{D}$, identify $\bb{Z}^s$ with $\bb{Z}^{Q(V)_0}$, and let $\wt{R}$ denote the projection $\bb{Z}^{Q_0}\rar \bb{Z}^{Q(V)_0}$, $\wt{R}(1_{i,\upalpha})=1_i$.  Then the parity statement follows from \eqref{eta_parity}, property (4) above, and the observation that $\upchi_Q=\wt{R}^*\lambda$.

If $Q(V)$ is acyclic, then $Q(V,P)$ is genteel by Corollary \ref{GenteelCor}, so the incoming walls listed in Properties (1) and (2) of $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ above are the only incoming walls of $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$.  The claim that the only incoming walls of $(R,F)_*\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ are as in \eqref{DWallsProp} follows using Lemma \ref{QuotientScat} (assuming we choose the representative of $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ to be saturated).

If we additionally have $p_i(t)=1$ for each $i$, then by Corollary \ref{MRcor}, we can represent $\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ so that each $p_v(t)$ as in Property (3) above has Lefschetz type.  Since in this case $F$ maps $x_{i,\upalpha}$ to $z^{v_i}$, all scattering functions of $(R,F)_*\f{D}_{\mathrm{Stab}}$ will still have Lefschetz type, as desired.

\[
\left(\begin{array}{cccc} \mathrm{Id}_{\upalpha\times\upalpha} & 0& \ldots & 0\end{array}\right)
\]
while $\cdot c$ acts  via the linear map $\bb{C}^{\upbeta}\rightarrow \bb{C}^{\upbeta}$ defined via the matrix 
\[
\left(\begin{array}{ccccc}  0&1&0&0&\ldots\\
 0& 0& 1 &0&\ldots\\
 &&\ldots&&\\
0&0&\ldots&0&1\\
\lambda_1&\lambda_2&\ldots&&\lambda_{\upbeta}
\end{array}\right).
\]
If $V$ is a submodule of $\rho$ of dimension vector $(x,y)$, the fact that $V\cdot \lp{2}$ is preserved by $\cdot c$ implies that $y\geq x+\upbeta-\upalpha$ whenever $x>0$.  Since $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),(x,y))=-\upalpha y +\upbeta x$, we have $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\underline{\dim}(V))=-\upalpha y\leq 0$ if $x=0$, and if $x> 0$, we have \begin{align*}
    -B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),(x,y))  & \leq -\upalpha x -\upalpha\upbeta+\upalpha^2+\upbeta x=(\upbeta-\upalpha)(x-\upalpha)\leq 0.
\end{align*} 
Hence, $\rho$ is $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)$-semistable.

In fact, if $x=\upalpha$, then $y=\upbeta$ and so $V=\rho$. Hence, if $V$ is a non-trivial proper submodule of $\rho$, then we must have $x<\upalpha$ and so if $\upalpha<\upbeta$ we find $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\underline{\dim}(V))<0$.  So $\rho$ is in fact $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)$-stable.  Moreover
\begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    If $\upalpha=\upbeta$, all indecomposable $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)$ King-semistable modules arise this way.  Since $\rho$ contains a $(1,1)$-dimensional representation spanned by the vectors $v'$ and $v$, where $v$ is any eigenvector of $\cdot c$ and $v'$ satisfies $v'\cdot a=v$, there are no $-B((1,1),\cdot)$ King-stable $(n,n)$-dimensional representations for $n\geq 2$.
    \item
    If $\upalpha=1$, all $-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)$ King-semistable (and hence stable) $(\upalpha,\upbeta)$-dimensional $\bb{C}Q$-modules arise this way.  As such, there is an isomorphism $\mathcal{M}_{(1,\upbeta)}^{-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)-sst}(Q)\cong \bb{A}^{\upbeta}$. Geometrically, this also follows from the fact that the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{(1,\upbeta)}^{-B(\underline{\dim}(\rho),\cdot)-sst}(Q)$ can be identified with the Hilbert scheme of $\upbeta$ points on $\bb{A}^1$, which is identified with $\mathrm{Sym}^{\upbeta}\bb{A}^1\cong\bb{A}^{\upbeta}$ via the Hilbert--Chow morphism. 
\end{enumerate}
We have drawn the diagram $\f{D}$ of Corollary \ref{2WallPos} in Figure \ref{scat_fig}.  One ellipsis in the diagram indicates that for every $n\in \bb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ there is a wall with function starting $\mathbb{E}(t^{-n}z^{(1,n)}+\cdots)$, a fact that we deduce from (2).  From (1) we deduce that there are no higher order terms on the wall through $(-1,-1)$, i.e. the $z^{(2,2)}$ coefficient is zero.  The grey region indicates that, because of the existence of the above stable modules, by Lemma \ref{dimension_lemma} there is a dense region of nonzero walls in the scattering diagram --- in fact, the existence of these stable modules implies that $z^{(\upalpha,\upbeta)}$ has a nonzero coefficient in the scattering function in which it appears for every $0<\upalpha<\upbeta$.

nodes.statement: Via Theorem and Lemma , the statement above regarding nonvanishing of the coefficients for z^(upalpha,upbeta) is equivalent to the existence of stable modules of dimension vector (upalpha,upbeta). So rather than using the above example to deduce the existence of such stable modules, one could hope to directly show the existence of the stable modules, and then deduce the nonvanishing of the coefficients from this. Indeed, as pointed out to us by Pierrick Bousseau, there is an argument taking as its inputs only results from the quiver literature and which demonstrates the existence of such stable modules, without invoking any DT theory or scattering diagram techniques.

Re-ordering the walls if necessary, we assume omega(v_1,v_2)=ninZ_geq 0. We also assume that n>0, since otherwise fD_in is already consistent. We construct a quiver Q via the following recipe. item First, we define quivers Q^(i), for i=1,2 by the rule: item If m_i=1 then Q^(i) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver Kr2, with vertices 1^(i) and 2^(i) and 2 arrows from 2^(i) to 1^(i). item If m_i=0 then Q^(i) is isomorphic to the quiver LQ0, with one vertex, denoted 1^(i), and no arrows. item We define Q' to be the disjoint union of Q^(1) and Q^(2). item We adjoin n arrows from 1^(2) to 1^(1) to Q', to form the quiver Q. Fix an integer kgeq 0, and denote by uppihspace0.05emcolon widehatG_Qrightarrow G_Q,k the projection defined as in S. Next, fix numbers 0leq epsilonll updeltall 1ll Mll N, which will depend on k. We define the stability conditions upzeta(pm) for Q as follows. item If m_1=1, we set upzeta(pm)(1^(1))=Mpmepsilon and upzeta(pm)(2^(1))=-M. item If m_1=0 we set upzeta(pm)(1^(1))=pm epsilon. item If m_2=1, we set upzeta(pm)(1^(2))=N and upzeta(pm)(2^(2))=-N. item If m_2=0 we set upzeta(pm)(1^(2))=0. Let upzeta be one of upzeta(pm). Let rho be a CQ-module, with dim(rho)leq k, satisfying the condition that each of the subquotients appearing in the Harder--Narasimhan filtration of rho with respect to the stability condition upzeta has slope contained in Icoloneqq [-updelta,updelta]. Then in particular, rho has slope contained in [-updelta,updelta]. It follows that if Q^(2) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver, the restriction of the dimension vector of rho to Q^(2) must be (a,a) for some ain Z_geq 0. Then the contribution of Q^(2) to the slope of rho is zero, whichever quiver Q^(2) is, and so if Q^(1) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver, the restriction of the dimension vector of rho to Q^(1) must be of the form (b,b) for some binZ_geq 0. Let rho be a CQ-module with dim(rho)leq k, and with the dimension vector of rho constant after restriction to Q^(1), and also constant after restriction to Q^(2). We claim that the following are equivalent item All of the subquotients appearing in the Harder--Narasimhan filtration of rho with respect to upzeta(-) have slope in I item The restrictions rho^(i) of rho to Q^(i) are upzeta(+) semistable for i=1,2 item All of the subquotients appearing in the Harder--Narasimhan filtration of rho with respect to upzeta(+) have slope in I. item[(1)Leftrightarrow (2)] The equivalence is trivial if one of rho^(1) or rho^(2) is trivial, so assume that they are both nontrivial. So rho^(2) is a proper nontrivial submodule of rho, and destabilizes it (for the stability condition upzeta(-)). In particular, picking rho'subsetrho^(2) to be the maximal submodule to attain the maximal slope of a submodule of rho^(2), rho' is the maximal destabilizing submodule of rho and it has slope in I if and only if rho^(2) is semistable (with respect to both stability conditions). Similarly, the maximal destabilizing quotient of rho with respect to upzeta(-) is a quotient of rho^(1), and it has slope in I if and only if rho^(1) is semistable with respect to both stability conditions. item[(3)Rightarrow (2)] If rho'subset rho^(2) was a destabilizing submodule with respect to upzeta(+), it would also be a submodule of rho with upzeta(+)-slope greater than updelta, which is impossible by the condition on rho. Similarly, if rho'subset rho^(1) was destabilizing, then rho'oplus rho^(2), with its natural CQ-module structure, would have slope greater than updelta. So we deduce that both rho^(1) and rho^(2) are semistable. item[(2)Rightarrow (3)] Say that rho^(1) and rho^(2) are semistable. Let rho'subset rho be the maximal destabilizing submodule with respect to the stability condition upzeta(+), i.e. the first non-trivial term in the Harder--Narasimhan filtration of rho. If Q^(2) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver, let (a,b) be the dimension vector of rho' restricted to Q^(2). Since this restriction is a submodule of rho^(2) we must have aleq b. On the other hand, since rho' destabilizes rho we must have ageq b. We deduce that a=b, and so whichever quiver Q^(2) is, the contribution of Q^(2) to the slope of rho' is zero. Now assume that Q^(1) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver. By the same argument, the dimension vector of rho', restricted to Q^(1), must be constant. We deduce that the slope of rho' lies within I. Applying the same argument to rho/rho', we see that the slope of all the subquotients in the Harder--Narasimhan filtration of rho belong to I. From (1)Leftrightarrow (3) we deduce that M^upzeta(+)_I(Q)=M^upzeta(-)_I(Q). Consider the case in which Q^(1) is the single vertex quiver, and write ein K for the generator corresponding to the vertex 1^(1). We have \[ upchi_wt,Kleft(bigoplus_vin Z_geq 0cdot eH_c(M^upzeta(pm)-sst_v(Q))_vir^*right)=E(x^e) \] by (). Now consider the case in which Q^(1) is isomorphic to the Kronecker quiver. Write e for the sum of the generators in K corresponding to the vertices 1^(1) and 2^(1). Then by () we have \[ upchi_wt,Kleft(bigoplus_vin Z_geq 0cdot eH_c(M^upzeta(pm)-sst_v(Q))_vir^*right)=E(x^e[2]_t). \] The same results hold for Q^(2); we let f denote the element in K defined analogously to e but for Q^(2). Applying () with upzeta=upzeta(-) we deduce that uppihspace0.05emleft(upchi_wt,Kleft(bigoplus_vin KH_c(M^upzeta(-)_I,v(Q),Q)^*_virright)right)=uppihspace0.05emleft(E([m_2+1]_tx^f)E([m_1+1]_tx^e)right). nodes.statement: We know from Lemma that T_k(fD_S) is a scattering diagram over fg_M_upmu_k(S),0^+,Uplambda. We will now show that the incoming walls of T_k(fD_S) are the same as the incoming walls of fD_upmu_k(S), and we will then show that T_k(fD_S) is consistent. Proposition then follows from the uniqueness statement of Theorem . Step 1, incoming walls coincide: Using the equivalence of Example (2), let us split up all walls (fd,f_fd) under consideration into their intersections (fdcap sH_k,+,f_fd) and (fdcap sH_k,-,f_fd), throwing away any empty intersections (and keeping only one copy of fd_k=fd_kcap sH_k,pm). Now since T_k,pm are linear and injective, it is clear that a wall of the form (fdcap sH_k,pm,f_fd) contains its direction -v_fd if and only if T_k(fdcap sH_k,pm) contains its direction T_k,pm(-v_fd). That is, T_k maps incoming walls to incoming walls and maps outgoing walls to outgoing walls. Next we check that the functions on the incoming walls of T_k(fD_S) match those on the incoming walls of fD_upmu_k(S). Consider an incoming wall (fd_icap sH_k,pm,f_fd_i) of the modified fD_S,in, where fd_i=e_i^perp and f_fd_i=Psi_t( z^v_i). The corresponding wall in T_k(fD_S,in) is (T_k(fd_icap sH_k,pm),Psi_t(z^T_k(v_i))) if ineq k, or (fd_k,Psi_t(z^-v_i)) if i=k. In any case, implies that this is the same as (T_k(fd_icap sH_k,pm),Psi_t( z^B_1(upmu_k(e_i)))), which is the corresponding initial wall of fD_upmu_k(S),in. We have thus shown that the incoming walls of T_k(fD_S) and fD_upmu_k(S) coincide. Step 2, T_k(fD_S) is consistent: Here we follow the strategy of . It suffices to check consistency of T_k(fD_S) around joints contained in e_k^perp because this is the only locus where T_k fails to be linear. For non-initial walls (fd,f_fd)in fD_Ssetminus fD_S,in, the vector v_fdin upsigma is not contained in an extremal ray of upsigma, i.e., is not equal to a multiple of any e_i. So fd=fd_k is the only wall with v_fd^Uplambdaperp=e_k^perp. I.e., fD_S has no walls contained in e_k^perp other than fd_k. Now, let fj be one such joint in e_k^perp. Let upgamma denote a small closed path around fj based in sH_k,-. To any finite order, we can consider a path upgamma=upgamma_4circ upgamma_3circ upgamma_2circ upgamma_1 such that: item upgamma_1 is a path starting in sH_k,- and immediately crossing fd_k, crossing no other walls, item upgamma_2 crosses every wall containing fj with interior in sH_k,+, but crosses no other walls, item upgamma_3 is a path starting in sH_k,+ and immediately crossing fd_k, crossing no other walls, and item upgamma_4 crosses every wall containing fj with interior in sH_k,-, returning to the initial point of upgamma_1. It is sufficient to check that uptheta_upgamma,T_k(fD_S)=uptheta_upgamma,fD_S, since we know the latter is the identity because fD_S is consistent. We know from Lemma \ref{Tkscat} that $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ is a scattering diagram over $\f{g}_{M_{\upmu_k(S),0}^+,\Uplambda}$.  We will now show that the incoming walls of $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ are the same as the incoming walls of $\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}$, and we will then show that $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ is consistent.  Proposition \ref{mut-inv} then follows from the uniqueness statement of Theorem \ref{KSGS}.

\textit{Step 1, incoming walls coincide:}  Using the equivalence of Example \ref{EquivEx}(2), let us split up all walls $(\f{d},f_{\f{d}})$ under consideration into their intersections $(\f{d}\cap \s{H}_{k,+},f_{\f{d}})$ and $(\f{d}\cap \s{H}_{k,-},f_{\f{d}})$, throwing away any empty intersections (and keeping only one copy of $\f{d}_k=\f{d}_k\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm}$).  Now since $T_{k,\pm}$ are linear and injective, it is clear that a wall of the form $(\f{d}\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm},f_{\f{d}})$ contains its direction $-v_{\f{d}}$ if and only if $T_k(\f{d}\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm})$ contains its direction $T_{k,\pm}(-v_{\f{d}})$.  That is, $T_k$ maps incoming walls to incoming walls and maps outgoing walls to outgoing walls.

Next we check that the functions on the incoming walls of $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ match those on the incoming walls of $\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}$.  Consider an incoming wall $(\f{d}_i\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm},f_{\f{d}_i})$ of the modified $\f{D}_{S,\mathrm{in}}$, where $\f{d}_i=e_i^{\perp}$ and $f_{\f{d}_i}=\Psi_t( z^{v_i})$.  The corresponding wall in $T_k(\f{D}_{S,\mathrm{in}})$ is $(T_k(\f{d}_i\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm}),\Psi_t(z^{T_k(v_i)}))$ if $i\neq k$, or $(\f{d}_k,\Psi_t(z^{-v_i}))$ if $i=k$.  In any case, \eqref{Tkei} implies that this is the same as $(T_k(\f{d}_i\cap \s{H}_{k,\pm}),\Psi_t( z^{B_1(\upmu_k(e_i))}))$, which is the corresponding initial wall of $\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S),\mathrm{in}}$.  We have thus shown that the incoming walls of $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ and $\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}$ coincide.

\textit{Step 2, $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ is consistent:} Here we follow the strategy of \cite[Proof of Thm. 1.24, Step II]{GHKK}.  
It suffices to check consistency of $T_k(\f{D}_S)$ around joints contained in $e_k^{\perp}$ because this is the only locus where $T_k$ fails to be linear.  For non-initial walls $(\f{d},f_{\f{d}})\in \f{D}_{S}\setminus \f{D}_{S,\mathrm{in}}$, the vector $v_{\f{d}}\in \upsigma$ is not contained in an extremal ray of $\upsigma$, i.e., is not equal to a multiple of any $e_i$.  So $\f{d}=\f{d}_k$ is the only wall with $v_{\f{d}}^{\Uplambda\perp}=e_k^{\perp}$.  I.e., $\f{D}_S$ has no walls contained in $e_k^{\perp}$ other than $\f{d}_k$.





Now, let $\f{j}$ be one such joint in $e_k^{\perp}$. Let $\upgamma$ denote a small closed path around $\f{j}$ based in $\s{H}_{k,-}$.  To any finite order, we can consider a path $\upgamma=\upgamma_4\circ \upgamma_3\circ \upgamma_2\circ \upgamma_1$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\upgamma_1$ is a path starting in $\s{H}_{k,-}$ and immediately crossing $\f{d}_k$, crossing no other walls,
    \item $\upgamma_2$ crosses every wall containing $\f{j}$ with interior in $\s{H}_{k,+}$, but crosses no other walls,
    \item $\upgamma_3$ is a path starting in $\s{H}_{k,+}$ and immediately crossing $\f{d}_k$, crossing no other walls, and    
    \item $\upgamma_4$ crosses every wall containing $\f{j}$ with interior in $\s{H}_{k,-}$, returning to the initial point of $\upgamma_1$.
\end{itemize}
 



It is sufficient to check that 
\begin{align}\label{thetaEq}
    \uptheta_{\upgamma,T_k(\f{D}_S)}=\uptheta_{\upgamma,\f{D}_S},
\end{align} since we know the latter is the identity because $\f{D}_S$ is consistent. 
We have
\begin{align*}
    {\uptheta_{\upgamma_1,T_k(\f{D}_S)}}&={\uptheta_{\upgamma_1,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}}} \\
    {\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,T_{k,+}(\f{D}_S)}}&=T_{k,+}(\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,\f{D}_S})  \\
    \uptheta_{\upgamma_3,T_k(\f{D}_S)}&=\uptheta_{\upgamma_3,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}} \\
    \uptheta_{\upgamma_4,T_k(\f{D}_S)}&=\uptheta_{\upgamma_4,\f{D}_S}.
\end{align*}

Recall that the existence of a compatible $\Uplambda$ implies that $\ker(B_{S,1})\cap M_{S,0}^+=\emptyset$, and similarly $\ker(B_{\upmu_k(S),1})\cap M_{\upmu_k(S),0}^+=\emptyset$.  Hence, $\hat{G}_S$ and $\hat{G}_{\upmu_k(S)}$ have trivial center, thus are isomorphic to their Adjoint representation.  It follows that elements of $\hat{G}_S$ and $\hat{G}_{\upmu_k(S)}$ are determined by their conjugation actions on $\Bbbk_{t,\upsigma}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$ and $\Bbbk_{t,\upmu_k(\upsigma)}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$, respectively, and in fact, these actions are already determined by their restrictions to monomials $z^m$ with $m\in \s{H}_{k,-}$.

Suppose $f\in \Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]$.  Then $T_{k,+}^{-1}(f)$ is also in $\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]\subset \Bbbk_{t,\upsigma}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$, hence $\mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,\f{D}_S}}(T_{k,+}^{-1}(f))\in \Bbbk_{t,\upsigma}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$.  We thus see that we can factor the conjugation homomorphism 
$$\left.{\mathrm{Ad}_{T_{k,+}(\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,\f{D}_S})}}\right|_{\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]}\colon \Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]\hookrightarrow \Bbbk_{t,\upmu_k(\upsigma)}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$$
into the composition $$\left.T_{k,+}\right|_{T_{k,+}^{-1}(\Bbbk_{t,\upmu_k(\upsigma)}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb)}\circ {\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,\f{D}_S}} \circ \left.T_{k,+}^{-1}\right|_{\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]}.$$



Let $\uptheta_{\f{d}_k}\coloneqq \uptheta_{\upgamma_1,\f{D}_S}=\Psi_t(z^{v_k})$, and let $\uptheta_{\f{d}'_k}\coloneqq  \uptheta_{\upgamma_1,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}}=\Psi_t(z^{-v_k})^{-1}$.  Note that $\uptheta_{\upgamma_3,\f{D}_S}=\uptheta_{\f{d}_k}^{-1}$, and similarly, $\uptheta_{\upgamma_3,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}}=\uptheta_{\f{d}'_k}^{-1}$.  Since $T_{k,-}=\mathrm{Id}$, we have $\uptheta_{\upgamma_4,\f{D}_{S}}=\uptheta_{\upgamma_4,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}}$.  In summary, we have on $\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M]$ that
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\upgamma,\f{D}_{\upmu_k(S)}}} =  \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\upgamma_4,\f{D}_{S}}}\circ \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}_{k}'}^{-1}} \circ (T_{k,+}\circ \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\upgamma_2,\f{D}_S}} \circ \left.T_{k,+}^{-1}\right)\circ \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}'_k}}.
\end{align*}

Hence, \eqref{thetaEq} will follow if we show that 
\begin{align*}
    T_{k,+}^{-1} \circ \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}'_k}}(z^m) = \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}_k}}(z^m)
\end{align*}
for all $m\in \s{H}_{k,-}$, i.e., $0<\langle -e_k,m\rangle = \Uplambda(v_k,m)$, cf.  \eqref{Lambda}.   
Applying \eqref{AdPsi}, we have
\begin{align*}
    T_{k,+}^{-1} \circ \mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}'_k}}(z^m) &= T_{k,+}^{-1}\left(z^m \prod_{k=1}^{|\Uplambda(-v_k,m)|} \left(1+t^{\mathrm{sgn}(\Uplambda(-v_k,m))(2k-1)}z^{-v_k}\right)\right) \\
    &= z^{m+\Uplambda(v_k,m) v_k} \prod_{k=1}^{|\Uplambda(v_k,m)|} \left(1+t^{-(2k-1)}z^{-v_k}\right) \\
     &= z^{m}t^{\Uplambda(v_k,m)^2} \prod_{k=1}^{|\Uplambda(v_k,m)|}  \left(z^{v_k}+t^{-(2k-1)}\right).  
\end{align*}
In the second equality, we applied $T_{k,+}^{-1}$ and used $-\langle e_k,m\rangle = \Uplambda(v_k,m)$  again.   We obtained the third equality by factoring $$z^{m+\Uplambda(v_k,m)v_k}=t^{\Uplambda(v_k,m)^2} z^mz^{\Uplambda(v_k,m)v_k}$$ and then distributing the last monomial.  Noting that $t^{\Uplambda(v_k,m)^2}=\prod_{k=1}^{|\Uplambda(v_k,m)|} t^{2k-1}$, we see that the last expression can be rewritten as
\begin{align}\label{thetadk}
     z^{m}\prod_{k=1}^{|\Uplambda(v_k,m)|} \left(t^{2k-1}z^{v_k}+1\right).
\end{align}
Since $\mathrm{sgn}(\Uplambda(v_k,m))=1$, we see using \eqref{AdPsi} again that this is indeed equivalent to $\mathrm{Ad}_{\uptheta_{\f{d}_k}}(z^m)$, as desired.

nodes.statement: Given a broken line upgamma with ends (p,Q) whose underlying map is upgammacolon (-infty,0]rar M_bbR, the underlying map for T_k(upgamma) is of course taken to be T_kcirc upgamma. Subdivide the domains of linearity of upgamma so that each lies entirely in either sH_k,+ or sH_k,-. For a domain of linearity Lsubset sH_k,pm, T_k takes the attached monomial c_Lz^m_L to T_k,pm(c_Lz^m_L). We wish to check that this gives a broken line. Let us assume that the representative of fD_S is chosen so that each scattering function is of the form Psi_t(t^2az^v) or Psi_t^2^r(t^2^r(2a+1)z^2^rv) for various ain bbZ, rin bbZ_geq 0, and vin M_S,0^+, as in Theorem . Let hatG_S^circ denote the subgroup of hatG_S generated by the scattering functions of fD_S, so Lemma ensures that T_k,pm take hatG_S^circ into hatG_upmu_k(S). For (fd,f_fd) a wall of fD_S, pin M, and epsilon=sgn(Uplambda(v_fd,m)), we see that T_k,pm(Ad_f_fd^epsilon (z^p)) = Ad_T_k,pm(f_fd)^epsilon(T_k,pm(z^p)). Indeed, by , Ad_f_fd^epsilon(z^p) and Ad_T_k,pm(f_fd)^epsilon(z^p) are both contained in Bbbk_t^Uplambda[M], so the equality follows from the fact that, since T_k,pm respects Uplambda, the maps T_k,pmcolon hatG_S^circrar hatG_upmu_k(S) and T_k,pmcolon Bbbk_t^Uplambda[M]rar Bbbk_t^Uplambda[M] are group and algebra homomorphisms which intertwine the actions of the groups on the algebras (cf. the proof of Lemma ). As a result, to show that T_k(upgamma) is a broken line for fD_upmu_k(S), it remains to check what happens when upgamma crosses e_k^perp. Let L_1,L_2 be consecutive refined domains of linearity of upgamma which lie on opposite sides of e_k^perp, and let c_iz^m_i denote the monomial attached to L_i. For L_1subset sH_k,-, we have Uplambda(v_k,m_1)>0, and so c_2z^m_2 is any term in Ad_Psi_t(z^v_k) (c_1z^m_1) = c_1z^m_1 prod_n=1^|Uplambda(v_k,m_1)| left(1+t^sgn(Uplambda(v_k,m_1))(2n-1)z^v_kright) where the equality is a special case of , with epsilon=1. Applying T_k,+, we have that T_k,+(c_2z^m_2) is a term in c_1z^m_1-Uplambda(v_k,m_1)v_k prod_n=1^|Uplambda(v_k,m_1)| left(1+t^sgn(Uplambda(v_k,m_1))(2n-1)z^v_kright). Applying the same manipulations which lead up to , we find that this is equal to c_1z^m_1 prod_n=1^|Uplambda(-v_k,m_1)| left(t^sgn(Uplambda(-v_k,m_1))(2n-1)z^-v_k+1right)=Ad_Psi_t(z^-v_k)(c_1z^m_1). Since the right-hand side is the corresponding wall-crossing for fD_upmu_k(S)=T_k(fD_S), it follows that T_k(upgamma) does in fact satisfy the correct bending rule. Similarly, if we instead had L_1subset sH_k,+, then T_k,-(c_2z^m_2)=c_2z^m_2 could be any term in the right-hand side of (although the sign of Uplambda(v_k,m_1) is now -1). On the other hand, if we apply T_k before the wall-crossing, we would have to apply T_k,+ to c_1z^m_1, yielding c_1z^m_1-Uplambda(v_k,m_1)v_k. One then computes that Ad_Psi_t(z^-v_k)(c_1z^m_1-Uplambda(v_k,m_1)v_k) =c_1z^m_1-Uplambda(v_k,m_1)v_k prod_k=1^|Uplambda(-v_k,m)| left(1+t^sgn(Uplambda(-v_k,m))(2k-1)z^-v_kright), and applying similar manipulations as before, noting that now Uplambda(v_k,m)<0 so z^-Uplambda(v_k,m_1)v_k=z^|Uplambda(v_k,m_1)|v_k, we find that this indeed equals the right-hand side of , as desired. We have thus shown that T_k takes broken lines to broken lines. That this is a bijection follows from noting that T_k^-1colon M_bbRrar M_bbR induces the inverse map on broken lines.

Here, $\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}\llb M^{\oplus_{_{S,S_{j}}}}\rrb$ is the completion of $\Bbbk_t^{\Uplambda}[M^{\oplus_{S,S_j}}]$ with respect to the maximal monomial ideal generated by $z^m$ with $m\in M^{+_{S,S_j}}\coloneqq M^{\oplus_{S,S_j}}\setminus M^{\times_{S,S_j}}$, where $M^{\times_{S,S_j}}$ is the monoid of invertible elements of $M^{\oplus_{S,S_j}}$. 

We see that $\s{A}_q^{\mathrm{can},S}$ and $\s{A}_q^{\mathrm{can},S_j}$ are both naturally contained in $\Bbbk_{\upsigma_{S,S_j},t}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$ --- between any two instances of a broken line $\upgamma$ crossing $e_j^{\perp}$, there must be an instance of $\upgamma$ crossing a wall $\f{d}$ with $v_{\f{d}}\in M^{+_{S,S_j}}$, so the completion in the $\pm e_j$ direction is not necessary.  Furthermore, since $T_j$ preserves $M^{+_{S,S_j}}$, it acts via homeomorphism and automorphism on $\Bbbk_{\upsigma_{S,S_j},t}^{\Uplambda}\llb M\rrb$ viewed as a topological $\Bbbk_t$-module. The claim follows. 

For the $\s{X}$-version, we first consider the compatible pair $(S^{\mathrm{prin}},\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}})$ for $\Uplambda^{\mathrm{prin}}$ as in \eqref{LambdaPrin} and recall the map $\upxi$ of Lemma \ref{xirho}.  By construction, $\psi_{\vec{\jmath},\mathcal{Q}}^{\s{A}^{\mathrm{prin}}}\circ \upxi = \upxi \circ \psi_{\vec{\jmath},\mathcal{Q}}^{\s{X}}$.  The $\s{X}$-version of the result thus follows from the $\s{A}^{\mathrm{prin}}$-version, and this is a special case of the $\s{A}$-version above.

For the final statement, we just have to check that $\Theta_{\s{V}}^{\mathrm{mid}}$ is preserved by $T_{\vec{\jmath}}^{\s{V}}$.  This again follows from Proposition \ref{MutInvBrokenLines} since $\Theta_{\s{V}}^{\mathrm{mid}}$ is defined in terms of the finiteness of certain sets of broken lines.
